# Introduction
Are you having a hard time switching from R to Python? Are the syntax errors making you crazy? Here is a step by step guide to help alleviate the frustration over syntax differences in R and Python. 

# How To
In this section, we will walk through an example data set, see common syntax differences, and finish with a cheat sheet guide of functions in R and their Python counterpart. 

## Worked Example
To practice the different syntax, we will work through an example using a data set of 2023 college football data. The data can be found in the GitHub repository data folder or on Kaggle at this [link](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/jeffgallini/college-football-team-stats-2019?resource=download&select=cfb23.csv). 

### Data Importing and Cleaning
Below we simply are loading the data in. We start by importing the pandas package which is equivalent to loading in a library such as `tidyverse` in R. We then load the data set in using `pd.read_csv`.
```{python}
# import pandas (equivalent to loading in libraries in R)
import pandas as pd
# import matplotlib for plotting (like ggplot but isn't included in pandas)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plot

# loading in data
data = pd.read_csv("data/cfb23.csv")

# check the head and tail of the data to make sure it loaded in correctly
data.head(6)
```

```{python}
data.tail(6)
```

After loading in the data, we want to check to make sure it was loaded in properly. We do this using `head` and `tail`. The syntax is just slightly different in Python as you can see above, however it is relatively similar. 
```{python}
# shape of the data frame
data.shape
```

`.shape` returns a tuple with dimensions of the pandas data frame. It is an attribute, not a function and that is why we don't use `()`. 
```{python}
# count number of na's for each variable
data.isna().sum()
```

Next we want to start running an analysis. To do so we need to do a little bit of data cleaning. For this analysis we will focus on teams, conferences, and their win-loss record. The data luckily has all of this for us but not in the correct format. Like in R, we can use Regex to handle the data extraction. We will do this below to extract the conference from the team name (`Team`) and the win loss record (`Win-Loss`). The dataset also includes over 150 columns which are not needed for our analysis. Below we also subset the data so that we only see the columns we care about.
```{python}
# add the conference variable
data["conference"] = (
    data["Team"]
    .str.extract(r"\(([^()]*)\)\s*$", expand=False)
)

# add the win and loss variables
data[["wins", "losses"]] = (
    data["Win-Loss"]
    .str.extract(r"^\s*(\d+)\s*-\s*(\d+)\s*$")
    .astype("Int64")
)

# calculate the win percentage
data["win_pct"] = (
    data["wins"] /
    (data["wins"] + data["losses"])
)

## check things worked by looking at just the selected columns head and tail
# select specific columns to use
check_cols = [
    "Team",
    "conference",
    "Win-Loss",
    "wins",
    "losses", 
    "win_pct"
]


# take all rows and just the columns in check_cols
football = data.loc[:, check_cols].copy()

# inspect head
football.head(5)
```

```{python}
# inspect tail
football.tail(5)
```

As we can see, the conference and win-loss record was properly extracted and can now be used for an analysis!

### Analysis
For our analysis we will look at the best teams and conferences based on win percentage. To start, let us look 
at which teams have the highest win percentage
```{python}
top_10_teams = football.nlargest(
    10, "win_pct"
)
top_10_teams
```

We see that we have 1 undefeated team in 2023 (Michigan). A big difference from how this works in R, is that you use `.nlargest` rather than sorting (`sort`) in descending order and then just printing only the first 10. This way is much simpler and cleaner. 

Because of the way the season works, there is a high chance there are ties in the win percentage. Python will just grab the first one it finds. Let's extend the list of top teams.
```{python}
# get the top 15 teams
top_15_teams = football.nlargest(
    15, "win_pct"
)

top_15_teams
```

Now that we have the top 15 teams, we see that there were three/four way ties for all of the last 13. It is important to extend the list of top teams since there was a tie and otherwise would have been missed. There could be more ties further down but for sake of space we will keep it at 15. 

Next we want to compare conferences. **Important Note:** this dataset is during 2023 which was the year where many schools switched conferences or were in the process so conference alignment does look different today. Let's see which conference has the highest win percentage.

```{python}
conference_summary = (
    football.groupby("conference", as_index=False)["win_pct"]
    .mean()
    .sort_values("win_pct", ascending = False)
)

conference_summary
```

We can see that the SEC is the top conference, in terms of win percentage. This is not the most accurate or best way to evaluate top conference but it can be used as a piece of an analysis. We will not analyze other metrics to evaluate the best conference. Instead, let's plot the analysis we have done!

Below we plot these top 15 teams.
```{python}
#| fig-alt: "A bar plot of the 15 top teams of 2023 based on win percentage, in descending order."
top_teams_plot = top_15_teams.sort_values("win_pct").plot.barh(
    x = "Team",
    y = "win_pct",
    legend = False
)

top_teams_plot.set_title("Top 15 College Football Teams by Win Percentage (2023)")
top_teams_plot.set_xlabel("Win Percentage")
top_teams_plot.set_ylabel("Team")
```

We can see that all of our top 15 teams are over 0.5 win percentage which would make sense for top teams. It is also important to see that there are many ties in the data since generally teams play the same amount of games each season leading to the percentages being the same. 

Next let's look at the top conferences plot.
```{python}
#| fig-alt: "A bar plot showing the average college football win percentage by conference in descending order for 2023."
conferences = conference_summary.sort_values("win_pct", ascending = False).plot.bar(
    x = "conference",
    y = "win_pct",
    legend = False
)

conferences.set_title("College Football Conferences by Average Win Percentage (2023)")
conferences.set_xlabel("Conference")
conferences.set_ylabel("Win Percentage")
```

This is just a nice way of visually comparing conferences average win percentages. 

Here we see that `matplotlib` is structured differently than a `ggplot`. `matplotlib` actually works a little bit closer to base R plotting. In `ggplot`, we use the `+` to add different elements of a plot. In base R you start a plot and then can add things to the plot after the plot is intitialized. This is the same idea for `matplotlib`. 

## Common Syntax Differences
This is not an exhaustive list of all syntax differences between the two languages, but this is a list of some of the more common ones I have ran into while switching from R to Python. 

### Booleans
In R, for booleans we capitalize the whole word (i.e. `TRUE`). In Python, we only capitalize the first letter (i.e. `True`). 

### Indexing
R has index starting at 1 while Python is indexed starting at 0. This is crucial to remember when trying to access elements of vectors.
Ex: `vec[1:5]` pulls the 1,2,3,4,5 elements in R. `vec[0:5]` will pull the first 5 elements (0, 1, 2, 3, 4) in python.

### Missing Value Checks
In R, we use `is.na(df$column)` to check for NA's. In Python, we use `df[column].isna()`.

### Methods vs. Attributes
In R everything done to an object is done in a function. This includes checking dimensions and types for data. For example, `dim(df)` return the dimensions of the data and `typeof(df$col)` returns what data type a column is. In Python, these types of metadata are accessed without parentheses. For example, `df.shape` returns the shape of the data frame as a tuple and `df["col"].dtype` returns the data type of the column. 

### Logic Negation
In R we use `!` to negate (`if (!is.na(df$col)){}`). In python we use `not` (`if not df["col"].isna().any():`). We also see here the syntax for `if` statements and `for` loops.

### Column Selection
With `dplyr` in R we can use the `select` function. For example, `select(df, col1, col2)`. In Python we have to use a list of strings with double brackets. For example, `df[["col1", "col2"]]`

### `for`, and `if`
In R we construct a `for` loop by doing: 
```R
for (variable in seq) { 
    #code for each iteration
}
```

In Python we construct a `for` loop by doing:
```python
for variable in iterable:
    #code for each iteration
    # make sure it is idented
```

In R we construct an `if` statment by doing:
```R
if (condition){
    # whatever you want to happen
} else if (condition 2){
    # whatever you want to happen
} else{
    # whatever you want to happen
}
```

In Python we construct an `if` statment by doing: 
```python
if condition: 
    # indented whatever you want to happen
elif condition: 
    # indented whatever you want to happen
else: 
    # indented whatever you want to happen
```


## Cheat Sheet Guide
| Operation | R (`dplyr`/ Base R) | Python (`pandas`) | Helpful Notes |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| Inspect types | `glimpse(df)` / `str(df)`| `df.info()` or `df.dtypes` | `.dtypes` has no parentheses |
| Select columns | `select(df, a, b)` | `df[['a', 'b']]` | Requires double brackets `[[]]` |
| Filter Rows | `filter(df, a > 5 & b < 10)` | `df[(df['a'] > 5) & (df['b'] < 10)]` | Must use `&` and warp conditions in `()` |
| Range filter | `filter(between(a, 5, 10))` | `df[df['a'].between(5, 10)]` | Inclusive on both ends by default |
| Distinct count | `n_distinct(df$col)` | `df['col'].nunique()` | Don't use `.count()` |
| Frequency table | `count(df, col)` | `df['col'].value_counts()` | Returns counts per unique value |
